Senses.Explanation: To illuminate or shine (照) and to function or act (用): illuminating and functioning. The pair is also the headword of Linji's four illuminate-and-function modes (四照用). Linji's recorded address lists them: sometimes illuminate first and then function; sometimes function first and then illuminate; sometimes illuminate and function at once; sometimes illuminate and function at different times (有時先照後用，有時先用後照，有時照用同時，有時照用不同時). It continues that when illumination comes first, a person is present, and when function comes first, a thing is present (先照後用有人在，先用後照有法在). The corpus expands the last two modes with concrete actions. Illuminating and functioning at once is compared to driving off the plowman's ox, snatching a starving person's food, breaking the bone for marrow, and pressing in the needle (驅耕夫之牛，奪饑人之食，敲骨取髓，痛下針錐). Illuminating and functioning at different times is described as question and answer, establishing host and guest, and mixing water with mud to meet people as events arise (有問有答，立主立賓，合水和泥應機接物). Counts for the four forms are: illuminating and functioning at once (照用同時), 320; at different times (照用不同時), 188; illuminating first and then functioning (先照後用), 191; and functioning first and then illuminating (先用後照), 185. Later masters repeat the same fourfold frame, and the question 'What is illuminating and functioning at once?' (如何是照用同時) receives a shout and a blow. The headword occurs 1,133 times in 208 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: A corpus-wide term and the head of Linji's four illuminate-and-function modes (四照用). Linji supplies the fourfold address, but the curated occurrences are catalogued retellings, later reuse, a raised exchange, and memorial prose, so MasterName is null. Compare the named set of four (四照用), killing and giving life (殺活), and guest and host (賓主).

Senses.Explanation: A child who tends cattle: a herdboy, cowherd boy, or oxherd boy. The term occurs 334 times in 139 allowlisted texts, and Chan records concentrate its distinctive use in oxherding songs, pictures, public questions, and verse. In Puming's ten oxherding verses, the boy holds the grass rope without slack and works all day; later, when there is no ox anywhere, the boy is idle, claps, sings under the moon, and still returns to “one further barrier.” Fenyang Shanzhao's Herdboy Song says that the boy does not copy texts or read a single graph, yet unfolds countless scrolls and handles question and answer. Asked “what is the herdboy's song?” Xuefeng Yicun dances and leaves the teaching hall. Jiashan Lingquan Ziying answers “who is the person within Jiashan's scene?” with “the herdboy sings in the open fields; the woodcutter laughs deep in the clouds.” Dizang Shouen, Danxia Zichun, Hongzhi Zhengjue, and Furong Daokai further place the boy in teaching-seat and portrait verse. Zen bends the ordinary cattle-tending child into a recurring actor in staged ox-and-herder sequences, direct interview answers, and teaching-seat songs; different stages of the same herdboy-and-ox deployment are not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: To look around is to turn and look at a person, direction, or assembly. The verb retains that visual sense in Emperor Suzong's complaint that Nanyang Huizhong does not look at him and in an unnamed monk's looking east and west for the absent Changqing Da'an. Chan records also make it a recurrent teaching-seat stage direction. At an opening of the hall Xuedou Chongxian “looked around at the assembly” (顧視大眾) before speaking; Yungai Zhiyong follows the look with a shout and questions concerning host and guest. In one encounter Mazu Daoyi merely looks, Yangshan Huiji comments on the look, and the exchange ends. Ciji Cong compresses speech and action still further: “then he looked around at the assembly and said, ‘stop!’” (乃顧視大眾曰休). Yulin Tongxiu looks left and right, strikes the staff, and leaves the seat (顧視左右，卓拄杖，下座). Thus an ordinary look is bent into an observable public-address action of the teaching seat; the entry does not assign the look an unspoken symbolic message.

Senses.Note: Zen bends two ordinary looking verbs and an exclamation into the stable monastic name for Yunmen's repeated encounter sequence. ‘Look—look!—hah!’ written with the first graph for ‘look!’ (顧鑒咦) and the same phrase written with its witness variant (顧鑑咦) are graph variants; ‘drawn look’ (抽顧) is the later shortened form. ‘Reflect’ is retained only as an alternate lexical possibility for ‘look!’ (鑒); the explicit narratives foreground Yunmen saying the word while looking at the recorded questioner, so ‘look!’ is primary. Later aggressive metaphors applied to the sequence are recorded as later comments, not its definition. Frozen-corpus concordance: 29 exact hits in 21 storage files representing 20 independent works.

Senses.Explanation: The expression names Yunmen’s sequence: he looks toward the interlocutor, says “Look!”, and cuts off the attempted answer with “Hah!” Yunmen’s own record describes the interaction: he sometimes looked toward the recorded questioner and said “Look!”; when the questioner prepared to answer, Yunmen said “Hah!” The monasteries consequently named Yunmen by this look-and-two-utterance sequence. A collected transmission states the same sequence and adds that Deshan Yuanming later removed the initial look and called the shortened form “drawn look.” Later texts use the compact phrase as a named case, ask how it operates at face-to-face meeting, and place it alongside Yunmen’s other characteristic responses. The punctuation and speaker sequence matter: this is a recorded look and two utterances, not an abstract three-word maxim.
